title: Synthesis I: Two Sources, Contrasting Viewpoints
goal: Combine two opposing op-eds into one written answer that represents both sides fairly and states, specifically, where they actually disagree — not just "some people think X, others think Y."

prompts: From memory: state the four obligations/checks a careful contract reader applies (Session 9).

vocab.def: combining information or viewpoints from more than one source into a new, coherent understanding — not just summarizing each one separately, side by side, and stopping
describing an opposing view the way its strongest supporter would recognize it, even if you disagree with it — the opposite of a straw man (Session 7)
the specific claim, fact, or value judgment where two sources actually part ways — as distinct from things they agree on, or issues neither addresses

facts: two well-argued essays on the same question often agree on more than they disagree on — the disagreement is usually narrower and more specific than "they disagree about phones" suggests.
representing an opposing view fairly is a skill separate from agreeing with it; a strong thinker can state the other side's best point better than a weak thinker can state their own side's.
prime.question: recall a real disagreement (with a parent, friend, or in the news) where, once you stated the other person's actual point instead of your assumption of it, the disagreement turned out to be narrower than you'd thought.
prime.intro: Two facts before you reread: (1) two well-argued essays on the same question often agree on more than they disagree on — the disagreement is usually narrower and more specific than "they disagree about phones" suggests. (2) representing an opposing view fairly is a skill separate from agreeing with it; a strong thinker can state the other side's best point better than a weak thinker can state their own side's. Orienting question: recall a real disagreement (with a parent, friend, or in the news) where, once you stated the other person's actual point instead of your assumption of it, the disagreement turned out to be narrower than you'd thought.

write.task: Write a synthesis paragraph (7–10 sentences) that: states what both essays agree on; states the specific, narrow point of disagreement; names what kind of disagreement it is; represents each side's strongest point fairly (in your own words, not a straw man); and ends with your own reasoned judgment — which you should be able to defend by naming the specific evidence that moved you, not just a preference. Use synthesis and point of disagreement correctly at least once each.

items.q: Does your Write to read answer state the specific disagreement (scope: in-class only vs. all-day) rather than a vague "some people disagree about phones"? Did you name the unaddressed equity point?

passages.title: Two op-eds on the same question
paragraphs: A Full-Day Phone Ban Goes Too Far

Nobody disputes that phones distract students during class — the attention research on that point is genuinely strong, and no serious opponent of a full-day ban argues students should be texting during a lesson. The real disagreement is narrower than full-day-ban advocates suggest: should phones also be banned during lunch and passing periods, when class isn't happening at all?

A full-day ban treats a fifteen-year-old checking a message from a working parent, or coordinating a ride home, the same as a student ignoring a teacher mid-lesson — as if all phone use, everywhere in the building, is equally harmful. It isn't. The in-class case is about protecting instructional time from a specific, measurable distraction. The lunch-period case is about something much softer and less measurable: a hoped-for increase in face-to-face conversation, based on informal staff impressions in a handful of districts, not the kind of large, controlled research that backs the in-class case.

There's also a real equity dimension full-day-ban advocates rarely address directly: students who work part-time jobs, who care for younger siblings after school, or whose parents' work schedules are unpredictable, use lunchtime phone access to coordinate real logistics — a ride, a shift change, a sibling pickup — not just social messaging. A full ban's "office stays reachable" answer assumes every urgent need is an emergency the office would even know to relay; a text about a changed pickup time is not an emergency, but it's still something a student needs to handle, and an office switchboard is a poor substitute for a two-line text a student can send in ten seconds between classes.

None of this means "no phone policy at all." A ban on phone use during instructional time, strictly enforced, addresses the actual, well-evidenced problem. Extending that ban into every unstructured minute of the day trades a strong, specific case for a much weaker, more speculative one — and does it by treating every student's non-class phone use as equally disposable, which for some students, it simply isn't.

questions.q: What do both essays agree on? Quote the sentence(s) that show the agreement most clearly.
Is the disagreement mainly factual, values-based, or about priorities? Defend your answer using both texts' actual content.
This essay raises an argument the original essay never addressed at all (not just answered weakly — never mentioned). What is it?

Think question: both essays agree the in-class attention research is strong. Given that, what's the actual, narrower question a school board would need to decide — and what additional evidence (not yet in either essay) would help settle it?

moves.title: synthesizing two sources
paragraphs: Reading two sources on the same question and writing one answer requires four steps: (1) identify what both sources agree on (often more than expected); (2) identify the specific point(s) where they genuinely disagree; (3) for each disagreement, note what kind of disagreement it is — a factual dispute (checkable), a values dispute (not resolvable by more facts alone), or a dispute about priorities (both facts might be true, but which matters more?); (4) write an answer that states both, fairly, before giving your own judgment.

roles.prompt: Which essay's evidence, overall, is stronger on the specific disagreement point (lunch/passing periods), and why?
What data would you want a district to collect before deciding?
Explain "represent fairly" using this second essay's fair treatment of the first essay's strongest point as the example.
Two sentences: agreement, then the actual disagreement.
